summary: The Guardian reports on an Amnesty International finding that Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance firm blacklisted by the US and flagged by the UK over the repression of Uyghurs, has cameras deployed across East Jerusalem and the West Bank. Amnesty warns these devices may feed Israeli police facial-recognition networks like Mabat 2000, restricting Palestinians' movement, protest and daily life. Hikvision gave no on-the-record response, and experts say its record shows it has not honored human rights commitments.
one_line: Amnesty found Hikvision cameras, from a firm tied to Uyghur repression, in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, aiding Israeli surveillance of Palestinians.
key_facts: Amnesty International's report 'Automated Apartheid', published in May, first revealed Hikvision cameras in the West Bank and documented facial-recognition and surveillance technology used to reinforce Israel's occupation.

Hikvision is based in Hangzhou, China, is one of the world's largest makers of video surveillance equipment, is blacklisted by the US and has been identified by the UK as a security threat for complicity in repression of the Uyghur minority.
Amnesty identified dozens of Hikvision devices in the old city of East Jerusalem, nearly 40 of them on security infrastructure and illegal settlements in the Silwan neighborhood.
The devices were operated by Israeli police and private settlers, and were mounted around Damascus Gate, the Armenian quarter, the Muslim quarter and Silwan.

Amnesty could not confirm facial recognition was activated on all identified products but said the cameras are at high risk of being connected to Mabat 2000, an Israeli police-run facial-recognition network spanning all of East Jerusalem.

Hikvision has marketed facial-recognition features claimed to automatically detect Uyghur people and to discern ethnicity, age and race, and enabled police clients to set alarms for protest activity such as 'unlawful assembly, procession, demonstration'.
Hikvision did not respond to Amnesty's report or give an on-the-record response, but previously told the Guardian it 'has never knowingly or intentionally committed human rights abuses itself'.
Conor Healy of IPVM said Hikvision's role in surveilling Muslims in Xinjiang and its failure to take accountability show it is 'not serious about ethics or protecting human rights'.
In 2021, the Washington Post revealed a database called Wolf Pack holding images and information on all 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank.
Amnesty's Digital Verification Corps verified 15 videos showing Palestinians being detained where surveillance technologies appeared to have been used for registration, identification or recording.

Matthew Mahmoudi of Amnesty said the technology restricts Palestinians' freedom of movement and access to work, education and medical facilities, and deters resistance to expanding illegal settlements.

The report is newly relevant after the 7 October Hamas attacks, which Israel said killed 1,400 people; since then more than 170 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank and at least 11 Palestinian communities displaced, per the Palestinian health ministry.
